content.thinking:
I need to be careful not to invent numbers or overstate certainty—duration should be framed as a lower bound, error rate as unknown, and the root cause tied to the flag toggle as only a probable correlation with limited confidence, since it was never actually tested. I'm now drafting the root cause, executive summary, and assumptions, trying to avoid naming specific components unless unavoidable, though the flag name itself may need to appear.

I'm sketching out the impact section: incorrect stored spend totals, possible display errors on account pages, no operational degradation, and unknown error rates since metrics couldn't be read during the outage window. For mitigation, I want to note that nothing was auto-remediated—the recommendation was to flip the flag off manually, with a draft fix opened but not merged, and that this stops further drift without fixing already-corrupted data, so a backfill would still be needed.

assumptions: The start of impact is taken from the oldest purchase the reconciliation check flagged (22 Sep 15:00 UTC); it is the earliest known bad record, not a proven first moment of corruption.

The link between the feature flag and the bad totals rests on timing correlation alone. The flag was never turned off, so we do not know that doing so stops the drift, and no bad total was traced through the new code path.

The incident is treated as ongoing because the service had not recovered by the last minute of metrics available. The true duration and total record count are unknown and could be larger than anything stated here.

No error rate or volume figure is given: the metrics for the incident window could not be read. The ~0.5-2.5% account-page ClientDisconnected errors in the logs are ordinary background noise and are assumed unrelated to the reconciliation failure.

An alternative candidate - the io-summary-cache dependency that holds shopper spend figures - was considered and rated low (~0.15), partly because the service register says the page renders correctly without it. It was not ruled out by evidence, only deprioritised.
The 0.01 hours the automation held the incident measures how quickly it responded and triaged, not how long the service was broken; it should not be read as a resolution time.
Whether shoppers actually saw incorrect figures, or whether the corruption is confined to stored totals not yet surfaced, was not verified.
The draft pull request opened by the code-fix agent has not been reviewed or merged, and its correctness is unassessed.
input.executive_summary: A routine integrity check found that the stored monthly spend totals shown to shoppers did not add up against the underlying purchase records. The bad data appears to begin with a purchase recorded on 22 September at 15:00 UTC; the alert did not fire until 29 September at 14:58 UTC, and the condition had not been corrected as of the last data we can see, so the affected period runs from 22 September through at least 29 September and is a floor rather than a measured span — it may well continue past that point. Throughout this time the shop itself behaved normally: pages loaded, requests succeeded, and there was no slowdown or outage, which is why nothing was noticed for a week. The visible effect is on correctness of figures rather than availability: any shopper whose totals were written during this window may have been shown a wrong spend figure, and any internal or financial reporting drawn from those totals over the same period should be treated as suspect. We cannot say how many shoppers or records were affected — the metrics needed to quantify that could not be read during the investigation. The automated responder investigated within about a minute, identified a recently enabled feature as the probable cause, and deliberately did not act on its own: turning the feature off would not produce any signal fast enough for the system to confirm the fix worked, so it handed the change to a person as a recommendation and opened a draft code fix. As of this writing the recommended change had not been applied. Two follow-ups are outstanding regardless of who applies it: switching the feature off only stops new bad totals from being written, so the week of already-written totals still needs to be recomputed and corrected, and the fact that a week of incorrect financial figures produced no alert until a periodic check caught it is itself worth addressing.
input.root_cause: Most likely cause, not confirmed: the `monthly-spend-feature` flag was switched on at 2026-09-22T14:58:50Z, enabling a new spend-total computation path, and the oldest purchase the reconciliation check flagged as wrong is dated 2026-09-22T15:00:00Z — essentially the same moment. The new path appears to have written incorrect spend totals while the service stayed healthy on every operational signal (flat per-minute metrics, no deploys in the lookback window), which is consistent with silent data corruption that only surfaces when a periodic integrity check runs. This is a correlation-based hypothesis (the investigator rated it ~0.78) and was never tested: no rollback was executed and no per-record comparison of old-path versus new-path totals was performed, so the causal link between the flag's logic and the bad totals remains unverified.
